newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Political brawl deadlocks Australian republic push.
newsitem.headline: Political brawl deadlocks Australian republic push.

text.p: A national convention on the question of whether Australia should become a republic was under threat on Thursday as government and opposition declared they could not accept each other's approach to choosing delegates.
The Liberal-National coalition government refuses to hold a compulsory national vote to select half of the delegates to the December conference.
But the Labor opposition said it would not accept either of two other methods -- a voluntary national ballot for the elected delegates or appointment of all members by the government.
"An all-appointed convention would be a farce, a sham and undemocratic," said Labor legal spokesman Nick Bolkus.

Labor, which wants Australia to drop Britain's Queen Elizabeth as head of state, combined with other leftist parties in the Senate on Wednesday to remove a non-compulsory vote from legislation to set up the December convention.
Voting in Australian elections is always compulsory.

But Prime Minister John Howard, a monarchist who is due to meet the queen on Friday during a visit to Britain, looked set to insist that the legislation not be tampered with and the government was planning to push the legislation back into the upper house next week.
"We'll send the bill back to the Senate next week," a senior government official told Reuters.
Under the legislation, the other half of the 152 delegates would be appointed by the government from the ranks of state and federal parliaments, Aboriginal and community groups.
The Australian republic debate has cooled greatly since former Labor prime minister Paul Keating began the push in 1992.
Howard defused the republican issue in the run-up to the 1996 general elections by promising to set up a national convention to discuss it.
The issue failed to gain much attention and Howard won the election on the basis of economic policies.
Opinion polls show that about half of Australian voters favour a republic but also that they think the country has more important issues to worry about. Many people do not care.

The Senate voted down the voluntary ballot, due in August, partly because it saw it as a first step towards ending compulsory voting in all elections, which would suit conservatives because they think their followers are more likely to vote of their own accord.
